lead: Rapid tooling uses additive manufacturing to make the tool — a mould insert, a die, a casting pattern or a jig — that then produces many parts by a conventional process. Rapid manufacturing uses the same AM machine to make the part that is sold, with no tool at all. Both exist because a hardened steel injection mould takes weeks and costs lakhs of rupees, while AM can deliver a working insert or pattern in days. They are used for low-volume plastic parts, casting patterns, bridge production before a hard tool arrives, and shop-floor jigs and fixtures.
prereq: You need: Chapter 7.1 for AM basics, Chapter 7.2 for the STL-to-part chain, Unit 1 for casting patterns and investment casting, and Unit 3 for injection moulding.

sections.h3: Tools, not parts: the two ideas

blocks.text: Rapid tooling means using an AM machine to make, or to help make, the tooling: a mould insert, a die, a casting pattern, a jig or a fixture. The tool then goes into a conventional machine — an injection moulding press, a casting line, a drill — and parts come out the usual way. AM is one link in the chain, not the chain.

Rapid manufacturing means the AM machine builds the part that is sold. No mould. The part is post-processed and shipped. The process chain is the same as in Chapter 7.2; only the destination of the output changes.

The split exists because tooling is the long pole. A hardened steel mould for a phone cover takes weeks of machining, EDM (Unit 6) and fitting, and costs lakhs of rupees. A printed insert or a printed pattern reaches the press in days for a fraction of that. On a small batch the tool cost cannot be recovered, so a cheap fast tool, or no tool at all, wins.

items: Rapid prototyping: the AM part is a model to look at and test.
Rapid tooling: the AM part makes other parts, in hundreds or thousands.
Rapid manufacturing: the AM part is the product.

sections.h3: Direct tooling: AM inserts and conformal cooling

blocks.text: In direct tooling the AM machine builds the tool itself. Powder bed fusion (Chapter 7.5) builds an injection mould cavity insert in tool steel or maraging steel powder. The insert is then heat treated, machined on its mating faces, and the cavity is polished.

The main gain is conformal cooling. Drilled cooling lines are straight, so thick corners stay hot while thin walls freeze fast. Uneven cooling warps the part and stretches the cycle. AM builds a channel that follows the cavity surface at a roughly constant offset — commonly 8 to 15 mm from the surface, 6 to 12 mm diameter — with round bends instead of drilled plugs.

Payoff: shorter cycle, flatter parts, less scrap. The worked example below turns a 30 s cycle into 20 s. Cost: the as-built channel surface is rough, so trapped powder must be blown out, and polishing the cavity costs extra.

items: Design the insert and the channel path that follows the cavity surface.
Build the insert by powder bed fusion.
Stress relieve and heat treat to the required hardness.
Clear unused powder from the cooling channels.
Machine the mating faces and polish the cavity.
Fit the insert into the bolster and run the mould.

sections.h3: Indirect tooling: patterns, soft moulds, bridge tools

blocks.text: Indirect tooling prints a pattern or a master, and a conventional route copies it into the working tool. The AM part never touches the final material.

Investment casting pattern (Unit 1): print the pattern in a wax-filled polymer, attach it to the tree, dip in ceramic slurry to build the shell, burn the pattern out, and pour. Complex geometry that would need a split wax die comes out in one piece.
Soft mould: cast silicone or epoxy around an AM master. The soft mould makes 20 to 100 polyurethane or wax parts — enough for design approval or a pilot batch.
Bridge tooling: an aluminium or soft-steel mould, often with AM inserts or made from an AM pattern, that supplies the first few thousand parts while the hardened production tool is being cut.

items: Soft mould for shape and fit checks in a rubber-like plastic.
Bridge tool when the part must reach the market before the steel tool.
Printed pattern when the part is metal and the batch is small.

sections.h3: Choosing: economics, batch size, material, surface

blocks.text: The choice is a cost-per-part sum.
cost per part = C_tool ÷ N + c_part
blocks.where: C_tool is the total tool cost in ₹, N is the batch size in parts, and c_part is the cost of one part on the machine (material, machine hour rate × cycle time, labour) in ₹.

blocks.text: As N grows the tool cost is spread thinner, so the tool with the longer life wins. Material narrows the choice: silicone moulds take only polyurethane and wax, aluminium bridge tools wear fast with glass-filled plastics, and AM steel inserts run common engineering plastics. Surface finish matters too — an AM insert needs polishing before the cavity is good enough for a visible part.

blocks.text: Jigs and fixtures are rapid tooling too: a printed drill jig or checking fixture for a curved sheet metal part is ready in a day, where machining one takes a week.

examples.question: A conformal-cooled AM insert replaces a drilled insert in an injection mould. The cycle time falls from 30 s to 20 s. The batch is 10,000 parts and the machine hour rate is ₹500. Find the machine time saved and the cost saved, and state one reason the saving may not be fully realised.
steps: Time saved per part = 30 s − 20 s = 10 s.
Total time saved = 10 s/part × 10,000 parts = 100,000 s.
Cost saved = 27.78 h × ₹500 per machine hour = ₹13,889, about ₹13,900.
Reason: the AM insert may need more frequent polishing or replacement, and its channels need cleaning, adding downtime not counted here.
examples.answer: Machine time saved is 27.78 h and the cost saved is about ₹13,889 (roughly ₹13,900) for the batch.

traps: Rapid tooling is not rapid prototyping. The machine is the same, but a tool makes many parts and a prototype makes none.
Indirect tooling still needs a conventional step: shell building, silicone casting or copying. If the AM machine made the mould cavity directly, it is direct tooling.
An AM steel insert is not a hardened H13 production insert. Its life is shorter, so never quote production-mould life for it.
Unit slip: seconds saved per part × number of parts gives seconds; divide by 3600 before multiplying by the rupee-per-hour rate.
Conformal cooling changes the cooling channel path, not the gating system or the part design.

quiz.q: Define rapid tooling and rapid manufacturing in one line each.
quiz.a: Rapid tooling: AM makes or helps make a mould, die, insert or pattern that then produces parts. Rapid manufacturing: AM makes the end-use part itself.

quiz.q: Why does a conformal cooling channel shorten the injection moulding cycle?
quiz.a: It follows the cavity at a constant distance, so thick and thin sections cool at similar rates; the whole part reaches ejection temperature sooner and warps less.

quiz.q: A conformal insert cuts the cycle from 45 s to 32 s on a 6,000-part batch. Machine hour rate is ₹400. Find the time saved and the cost saved.
A customer needs 500 ABS covers in three weeks, and 50,000 more over the year. Which tooling route do you propose and why?
quiz.a: A hardened steel tool cannot be ready in three weeks, so use an aluminium bridge tool or an AM steel insert for the 500 covers and start the steel tool in parallel. The cost-per-part rule C_tool/N + c_part shows the bridge tool is dearer per part but avoids a late launch; ABS runs in both tools.
A provisional mould, often aluminium or with AM inserts, that makes the first few thousand parts while the production tool is being built.

quiz.q: Why must an as-built AM mould insert be polished before use?
quiz.a: Powder bed fusion leaves a rough surface, roughly 5-15 µm Ra; that roughness would print onto every plastic part and the part would stick in the cavity.

quiz.q: Tool cost is ₹1,20,000 for a batch of 500 parts and the machine cost is ₹35 per part. Find the cost per part.
quiz.a: Tooling share = 1,20,000 ÷ 500 = ₹240 per part. Total = 240 + 35 = ₹275 per part.

beyond: Not for the exam. Conformal cooling paths are now optimised by mould-filling simulation before the insert is built. Some inserts carry thermocouples printed into the steel so cavity temperature is logged during every cycle. Hybrid machines build the insert and then machine the cavity in the same setup. Research follows two lines: harder AM tool steels, and moulds with printed sensors. Search 'conformal cooling mould insert', 'bridge tooling' and 'hybrid additive manufacturing mould'.
